metadata.role: single source of truth for caption generation, caption validation, instruction-dataset construction, fine-tuning, evaluation, and paper
metadata.provenance: Rebuilt from the original PlantDx DKB for the new tomato-only dataset. Scientific descriptions are curated from authoritative plant-pathology and extension sources. Contains no image analysis, synthetic labels, or VLM-generated content.
metadata.observability_constraint: Captions must describe ONLY features visibly present in the image. This dataset contains both leaf and fruit classes, so the constraint is image-grounded rather than leaf-only. Do not infer unseen organs, symptoms, severity, causal agents, vector transmission, internal tissue damage, yield effects, or management outcomes.
metadata.pest_vs_pathogen_note: Aphid, Fruit Borer, Leaf Miner, Mealy Bugs, and White Fly are pest classes. Use feeding/mechanical-damage vocabulary rather than infection/pathogen/lesion vocabulary. Leaf_Curl is a visual phenotype and must not automatically be mapped to a specific virus.
documented_taxonomic_disagreements: Early blight is associated with closely related Alternaria taxa; the dataset class remains disease-level.
Target spot is retained at the dataset disease level and is not over-resolved beyond the class label.
Leaf_Curl is intentionally treated as a visual phenotype rather than automatically assigned to TYLCV.
Pest classes represent visible infestation or feeding damage rather than pathogen disease.
Fruit Borer is documented with Helicoverpa armigera as the principal Indian tomato reference, but the image class itself does not prove species identity.

diseases.taxonomy_note: Pest category rather than a single resolved species. Do not infer aphid species from the dataset label alone.
environmental_conditions: lush nitrogen-rich growth can favor buildup
diseases.disease_progression: Small colonies feed on soft tissue; heavy feeding can cause distortion/curling and yellowing. Honeydew may accumulate and support superficial sooty mold.
primary_symptoms: small soft-bodied pear-shaped aphids when visible
clustered feeding on tender growth or leaf undersides
secondary_symptoms: sticky honeydew or superficial dark coating when visible
lesion_morphology: NOT pathogen lesions; diffuse feeding injury and/or visible insect colonies
diseases.lesion_size: usually a few millimeters or less; image-dependent
leaf_margin_changes: curling/distortion may occur in tender growth
leaf_curling: curling or puckering when feeding is heavy
necrosis: not characteristic; secondary tissue darkening may occur
chlorosis: yellowing may develop with heavy feeding
diagnostic_visual_features: clustered aphids and associated leaf distortion
recommended_caption_vocabulary: a tomato leaf or shoot with visible aphid colonies and feeding-related distortion
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered aphid-management options only after scouting confirms a damaging population.

diseases.taxonomy_note: Early blight is associated with closely related Alternaria taxa; the dataset class remains at disease level.
diseases.disease_progression: Fruit lesions are typically sunken, dry/leathery and dark, often with concentric patterning; early blight can also affect leaves and stems.
primary_symptoms: dark brown to black sunken fruit lesions
concentric ridges/ring pattern may be visible
lesions often near the calyx/stem end
secondary_symptoms: fruit deterioration or drop in advanced disease
lesion_distribution: may occur on other fruit surfaces

mild: one or a few small dark spots
moderate: enlarging sunken lesions with concentric ridges

diagnostic_visual_features: sunken dark lesion with dry surface and concentric pattern
recommended_caption_vocabulary: a tomato fruit with a dark sunken dry lesion, optionally showing concentric ridges near the calyx
management_practices: manage volunteer tomato and solanaceous hosts
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered fungicide recommendations when disease is confirmed; do not prescribe from an image alone.

diseases.taxonomy_note: TNAU identifies Helicoverpa armigera as a major tomato fruit borer in India. The broader dataset class does not prove species identity for every image.
environmental_conditions: adult moth activity and egg laying
diseases.disease_progression: Larvae feed on tender foliage initially and then bore into fruit. Characteristic damage is a circular bore hole with internal feeding; frass may accumulate around the opening.
primary_symptoms: circular bore holes in tomato fruit
frass/fecal pellets around openings when visible
secondary_symptoms: fruit deformation or loss of marketable tissue
lesion_morphology: NOT pathogen lesions; mechanical feeding holes and chewed tissue
diseases.lesion_size: bore holes commonly several millimeters or larger; image-dependent
lesion_distribution: near calyx or other feeding sites
necrosis: secondary darkening around damaged tissue may occur

severe: extensive feeding damage with multiple openings and tissue loss

diagnostic_visual_features: bore hole with surrounding feeding damage
recommended_caption_vocabulary: a tomato fruit showing a circular feeding hole or chewed tissue associated with fruit borer damage
management_practices: collect and destroy damaged fruit and visible larvae
treatment_recommendations: Follow current local IPM and pesticide-label guidance; treatment should be based on scouting and pest identification.

diseases.taxonomy_note: No pathogen or pest is assigned to the healthy class.
primary_symptoms: absence of visible lesions, holes, rot, or abnormal surface damage
texture_changes: normal smooth or naturally textured fruit surface
severity_indicators: absence of visible disease, pest, feeding, cracking, rot, or abnormal discoloration
key_differentiating_features: no obvious pathological or pest damage
recommended_caption_vocabulary: an intact healthy tomato fruit with a normal visible surface
treatment_recommendations: none required for the healthy class

diseases.taxonomy_note: No pathogen or pest is assigned to the healthy class.
primary_symptoms: uniform green intact pinnately compound leaf
slight surface pubescence may be visible
severity_indicators: absence of spots, lesions, yellowing, mottling, webbing, coating, galls, cutting, or distortion
recommended_caption_vocabulary: a healthy tomato leaflet with uniform green coloration, intact serrated margins, and normal venation

diseases.taxonomy_note: Oomycete pathogen. Disease-level identification is appropriate for the dataset class.
diseases.disease_progression: Small water-soaked areas rapidly enlarge into irregular purple-brown/oily blotches. Grayish-white sporulation may occur on the underside; tissue collapses rapidly.
primary_symptoms: large irregular water-soaked or greasy blotches
white to grayish downy sporulation on the underside when visible

moderate: enlarging greasy blotches with underside sporulation
severe: large coalesced dark blotches, collapse and defoliation

recommended_caption_vocabulary: large irregular water-soaked grayish-green blotches, sometimes with white downy growth on the underside
treatment_recommendations: Use locally labeled late-blight management products and resistance-management guidance; image alone is not a treatment prescription.

diseases.taxonomy_note: The class name describes a visual phenotype and does not by itself identify TYLCV or another virus.
environmental_conditions: biotic or abiotic stress may produce curl
diseases.disease_progression: Leaves become curled, cupped, crumpled or distorted. Yellowing may accompany deformation, but the class remains visually defined.
lesion_morphology: deformation rather than a defined lesion
lesion_distribution: often most visible on young growth when present
necrosis: none characteristic unless secondary tissue death is visible

severe: pronounced curling, crumpling and marked deformation

key_differentiating_features: visible deformation is the defining feature
do not infer causal virus from curl alone
recommended_caption_vocabulary: tomato leaflets showing visible curling, cupping, or crumpled distortion
treatment_recommendations: Treatment depends on the underlying cause; do not prescribe a virus treatment from the image alone.

diseases.taxonomy_note: TNAU identifies Liriomyza trifolii as serpentine leaf miner on tomato in India.
diseases.disease_progression: Larvae tunnel within leaf tissue, producing pale serpentine mines. Mines widen as larvae grow; heavy infestations can dry and drop leaves.
primary_symptoms: larva or pupa may be visible at suitable resolution
secondary_symptoms: drying and leaf drop under heavy infestation
lesion_morphology: internal feeding mine; not a pathogen lesion
diseases.lesion_size: narrow trail that widens along its course
leaf_margin_changes: not usually margin-specific; larva may exit through a slit

mild: one or a few narrow mines
severe: dense/coalescing mines with drying or defoliation

recommended_caption_vocabulary: serpentine translucent feeding mines winding through the tomato leaf
management_practices: remove heavily mined leaves where appropriate
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered pest-management recommendations based on scouting and pest identification.

diseases.taxonomy_note: Pest family-level visual category; species should not be inferred from the class label alone.
diseases.disease_progression: Mealybugs colonize protected surfaces and feed on sap. Waxy/cottony material and honeydew may accumulate; heavy feeding can distort or yellow foliage.
primary_symptoms: clustered feeding on protected surfaces or leaf undersides
secondary_symptoms: sticky honeydew and superficial sooty coating when visible
lesion_morphology: NOT pathogen lesions; visible pest colonies and feeding-associated surface changes
diseases.lesion_size: usually a few millimeters or less

severe: dense colonies with extensive wax/honeydew and distortion

recommended_caption_vocabulary: a tomato plant surface showing visible pale mealybugs or cottony waxy colonies
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered mealybug-management options after pest identification and scouting.

diseases.taxonomy_note: Highly polyphagous fungus; retain the dataset disease label rather than over-resolving taxonomy.
diseases.disease_progression: Small dark spots enlarge into brown lesions with subtle concentric rings and lighter centers. Lesions can coalesce, causing blighting and defoliation.
lesion_morphology: dry necrotic lesions with subtle concentric zonation
diseases.lesion_size: pinpoint early spots to larger coalescing lesions

moderate: enlarging lesions with subtle concentric rings and pale centers

key_differentiating_features: absence of pycnidia as defining feature
diagnostic_visual_features: fine concentric-ring lesions with pale centers
recommended_caption_vocabulary: brown lesions with subtle concentric rings and pale centers scattered across the tomato leaf
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered fungicide recommendations and resistance-management guidance; image alone is not a treatment prescription.

diseases.taxonomy_note: Several whitefly species infest tomato; retain the class at the visual pest level rather than inferring species from an image alone.
diseases.disease_progression: Adults and nymphs feed on phloem. Feeding can cause yellowing and curling; honeydew can make surfaces shiny and support superficial sooty mold. Some whiteflies vector viruses, but transmission must not be inferred from visible insects.
primary_symptoms: fine yellowing or stippling from feeding
secondary_symptoms: black superficial sooty mold when visible
lesion_morphology: NOT pathogen lesions; feeding damage and/or visible whitefly stages

moderate: clustered whitefly stages with visible yellowing

key_differentiating_features: white adults or pale nymphs on underside
whitefly adults fly readily when disturbed
diagnostic_visual_features: whitefly adults/nymphs and fine feeding-related yellowing
recommended_caption_vocabulary: small whiteflies or pale nymphs visible on the tomato leaf, with fine feeding-related yellowing when present
management_practices: monitor leaf undersides and field margins
treatment_recommendations: Use locally registered whitefly-management options after scouting; do not assume virus transmission from visible whiteflies alone.
